title: The crying baby
hookLine: Shneur Zalman leaves his prayer to rock a crying baby his absorbed son never heard

cards: Someone so deep in their laptop they don't hear their name called three times. A parent on the phone while a toddler tugs and tugs at their sleeve. Maybe that someone was you.
Deep focus is a gift. It's how books get written and problems get solved. But it has a shadow.
Today's story is about a great scholar, lost in holy study, who missed a sound that mattered more, and about his father, who didn't.

teach.b: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi founded the Chabad movement and wrote the Tanya, the book at its heart. The story is told that he lived in a house with his son, Dov Ber, who would later lead Chabad after him.

teach.h: A SON TOO ABSORBED TO HEAR.
teach.b: One night Dov Ber was downstairs, completely absorbed in study. In the same room, his baby fell out of the cradle and began to cry. Dov Ber didn't hear a thing.
Upstairs, Shneur Zalman was deep in his own study and prayer. He heard the crying. He stopped, came down the stairs, picked the baby up, soothed the child, and laid it back in the cradle.
Afterward, the father spoke to him. However lofty your learning, he said, if it keeps you from hearing a child cry, something has gone wrong.
Look who's saying it: not a critic of study, but the founder of a movement built on deep, intense contemplation. He isn't saying stop learning.
He's saying learning that makes you deaf to a crying child has lost its way.
The Talmud says something in the same spirit: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, based on Abraham leaving God's company to run to three strangers.
Holiness that can't hear a baby isn't finished yet.

how: Chabad Hasidim tell this story about their first and second rebbes, and it is retold in Jewish homes and schools as a reminder that study and prayer should not make a person deaf to others.

o: the son who studied on and never heard the baby
the founder of Chabad and author of the Tanya
a rabbi who wrote the Talmud's laws on guests

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the story teaches that study isn't important
it's told about the founder of a movement devoted to study. it says learning must still hear.
Shneur Zalman was in the middle of his own study and prayer when he heard
he stopped, came down, and comforted the child.
the Talmud says welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence
it learns this from Abraham leaving God to greet three strangers.

games.q: you're deep in prayer upstairs. downstairs, a baby is crying, and its father hasn't noticed. what do you do?
o: go down and comfort the baby.
shout down for someone to deal with it.
games.why: Shneur Zalman stops, goes down, and soothes the child himself. then he tells his son: learning that can't hear a crying child has gone wrong.

practice: For a moment, listen not to your thoughts but to the room: the sounds outside, someone nearby, your own body, thirsty, tired or tense.
Then think of the people around you today, and who might be tugging at your sleeve, quietly, unnoticed. Pick one, and if you pray, pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Shneur Zalman, who stopped his own holy study to comfort a crying baby his son never heard. Holiness that hears.

carryVoice: Your line: the crying child first. The work can wait; the crying can't. Day three hundred six.
